newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin keeps cabinet on edge over reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin keeps cabinet on edge over reshuffle.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin had almost Russia's entire cabinet on tenterhooks on Wednesday after ordering a reshuffle in which no minister is safe except the prime minister and his newly appointed first deputy.

Yeltsin, unveiling the gradual shake-up agonisingly slowly, told Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to present proposals for the changes within a week but made clear new First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais would stay on.

Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and recently-promoted Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov can also sleep relatively soundly, but the nightmare goes on for more than 30 ministers already awaiting their fate for more than two weeks.

"It is not clear who will join the government other than the promises that they will be 'young and energetic'," Grigory Yavlinsky, leader of the liberal Yabloko political group, told Interfax news agency.

It is not clear how many ministers Yeltsin will replace. But the reshuffle has the clear aim of showing the president is firmly in charge after spending the best part of eight months out of the Kremlin with heart problems followed by pneumonia.
Yeltsin, 66, made clear he wanted a reshuffle at a meeting with Chernomyrdin on February 24 at which he criticised the government's failure to pay wages and pensions on time.
He demanded sweeping changes in a state of the nation speech on March 6 and appointed Chubais, until then the chief of his Kremlin administration, on March 7.

The appointment of Chubais, widely regarded as a brilliant administrator and an uncompromising liberal reformer, has been applauded by Western economists but criticised by Yeltsin's political opponents.

Chubais is hated by the opposition communists for masterminding Yeltsin's successful re-election campaign last year and for his role in overseeing privatisation, in which they say state assets were sold off cheaply.
"It (Chubais' appointment) will bring nothing in moral, political or economic terms," extreme nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky said.
Others were waiting to see what else Yeltsin had up his sleeve before deciding on the wisdom of the Kremlin leader's latest political gambit.
"It (the reshuffle) is necessary for the country, the economy and the people...Let's hope it brings some results," Gennady Burbulis, Yeltsin's former state secretary, told commercial NTV television.

All ministers dealing with the economy and social policy have some cause for concern in moves which Yeltsin hopes will ease tension over a huge backlog in wages and pensions which has prompted plans for nationwide protests on March 27.
Desperate pensioners in one region northwest of Moscow blocked a railway line for more than five hours on Tuesday to demand their unpaid pensions.
Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, 60, is also in the firing line. Yeltsin has told him to stop "whining" and to get on with much delayed military reforms.
Yeltsin has also begun changing his presidential team. He named 39-year-old former journalist Valentin Yumashev on Tuesday to replace Chubais as head of the Kremlin administration.
He also appointed Marshal Yevgeny Shaposhnikov, 55, the last Soviet defence minister, to be a Kremlin aide overseeing Russia's declining civil aviation and space sectors.
